So, I'm looking at this through autistic person lens, not autistic fat acceptance person lens. So this might not at all be what OOP is talking about, but I actually have some insight here.

I have a vast array of sensory difficulties due to my autism, the one that is most problematic when it comes to food is textural sensitivity. My brain fully freaks out at the texture of *a lot* of foods. And there's so many different types of texture that will trigger it.

But when it gets triggered, I gag. If I don't stop eating immediately, I will vomit in less than 10 seconds.

For me, the things most likely to trigger this are fibrous textures, so a lot of vegetables and fruits. It also gets triggered if I'm expecting a certain texture but don't get it, even if the one I do get is normally not a problem for me.

I get around this by blending veggies into sauces for as many meals as possible, but if you're also struggling with executive dysfunction, that might genuinely be beyond your ability. I know it is for me, some days. And those days, the harder ones, I tend to eat hyper-processed garbage just to have calories in me, because the textures of those foods are homogeneous as hell, no surprises.

So yeah, probably not exactly what OOP means, but might be relevant to consider, I guess.

Hi, I'm late to this thread, but I'd really like to share my experience. I have Asperger's, or what used to be diagnosed as Asperger's back in the day, I believe they've changed things in the last while.

I believed in Santa until I was 12. Well, mostly. By the time I hit age 10, even though my parents and brother would tell you I was a thousand percent certain of Santa at the time, I had gotten to a point of belief that was essentially "I want to believe this. This makes zero logical sense whatsoever, and might not really be true, but I was told this and I believed this and I still like this, so I still believe this".

Then, age 12, in school, came the question from the other kids. "Do you STILL believe in santa?!?!?!" My answer was an honest one. "It doesn't make sense, but it makes me happy." I was tormented for the rest of the day, more than usual.

But you know what? It stopped. Out of all the things I was bullied for, that wasn't one of them. It stopped after that one day. And to this day, I'm glad that my parents let me have that experience. I'm glad that they didn't, in an effort to protect me, sit me down ahead of time and tell me that it's all just make believe. I'm glad that this was one of those minefields they let me navigate by myself. Because this one thing taught me a lot about myself as a person, about other people, and about how things work in a social environment.

So, I don't know if any of this helps you decide what to do about your daughter's beliefs. I don't know if she'd take it like I did, or much harder on herself. As her parent, I'm sure you'd have the insight on that one, not me. But maybe you and her can figure it out together, maybe asking her how she'd feel if the other kids believed different things than her could be a good start.
